paragraphs: We have no well-documented records of Rome’s earliest period. Most of the stories told about it are very probably fables. In general, the most instructive part of any people’s history, the part about how it was founded, is the part we know least about. Experience shows us every day what causes lead to the revolutions of empires. But since no new peoples are formed now, we have almost nothing but guesswork to explain how they were created.

The customs we find established show at least that those customs had an origin. The traditions that trace back to those origins, that have the greatest authorities behind them, and that the strongest proofs support, should be accepted as the most certain. These are the rules I have tried to follow in asking how the freest and most powerful people on earth exercised its supreme power.

After the foundation of Rome, the newborn republic, that is, the army of its founder, made up of Albans, Sabines and foreigners, was divided into three classes. From this division they took the name of _tribes_. Each of these tribes was split into ten _curiæ_, and each _curia_ into _decuriæ_, headed by leaders called _curiones_ and _decuriones_.

In addition, a body of one hundred _Equites_, or Knights, called a _century_, was taken from each tribe. This shows that these divisions, which a town had no need of, were at first purely military. But an instinct for greatness seems to have led the little township of Rome to equip itself in advance with a political system fit for the capital of the world.

This original division soon produced an awkward situation. The tribes of the Albans (Ramnenses) and the Sabines (Tatienses) always stayed the same size, while the tribe of the foreigners (Luceres) kept growing as more and more foreigners came to live in Rome, so that it soon outstripped the others in strength. Servius fixed this dangerous flaw by changing the basis of the division. He abolished the division by race and put in its place a new one, based on the quarter of the town each tribe lived in. Instead of three tribes he created four, each occupying one of the hills of Rome and named after it. In this way he corrected the inequality of the moment and also provided for the future. And so that the division would be one of persons as well as of places, he forbade the inhabitants of one quarter to move to another, which prevented the races from mixing.

He also doubled the three old centuries of Knights and added twelve more, still keeping the old names. By this simple and prudent method he made a distinction between the body of Knights and the people, without a murmur from the people.

To the four urban tribes Servius added fifteen others, called rural tribes because they were made up of those who lived in the country, divided into fifteen cantons. Later, fifteen more were created, and the Roman people finally found itself divided into thirty-five tribes, as it remained until the end of the Republic.

The distinction between urban and rural tribes had one effect worth mentioning, both because it has no parallel anywhere else and because Rome owed to it the preservation of her morals and the growth of her empire. We would have expected the urban tribes to soon monopolize power and honors, and to lose no time in bringing the rural tribes into disrepute. What happened was exactly the reverse. The taste of the early Romans for country life is well known. They owed this taste to their wise founder, who joined rural and military labors with liberty, and, so to speak, banished to the town the arts, crafts, intrigue, fortune and slavery.

Since all of Rome’s most illustrious citizens lived in the fields and farmed the land, people grew used to looking there, and only there, for the mainstays of the republic. This way of life was the way of the best patricians, and everyone honored it. The simple and hard-working life of the villager was preferred to the lazy and idle life of the _bourgeoisie_ of Rome. A man who in the town would have been a wretched proletarian became, as a laborer in the fields, a respected citizen. Not without reason, says Varro, did our great-souled ancestors establish in the village the nursery of the sturdy and valiant men who defended them in time of war and fed them in time of peace. Pliny states plainly that the country tribes were honored because of the men who made them up, while cowards whom people wished to dishonor were transferred, as a public disgrace, to the town tribes. The Sabine Appius Claudius, when he came to settle in Rome, was loaded with honors and enrolled in a rural tribe, which later took his family name. Lastly, freedmen always entered the urban tribes and never the rural ones. Nor is there a single example, in the whole history of the Republic, of a freedman reaching any magistracy, even though he had become a citizen.
This was an excellent rule. But it was carried so far that in the end it led to a change in the political system, and certainly to an abuse.

First, the censors had long claimed the right to transfer citizens arbitrarily from one tribe to another. They then allowed most people to enroll themselves in whatever tribe they liked. This permission certainly did no good, and it also took away one of the censorship’s greatest resources. Moreover, the great and powerful all had themselves enrolled in the country tribes, while the freedmen who had become citizens stayed with the common people in the town tribes. As a result, both kinds of tribe soon lost any local or territorial meaning. They became so mixed up that the members of one could not be told from those of another except by the registers. The idea of the word _tribe_ thus became personal instead of real, or rather came to be little more than a fantasy.
It also happened that the town tribes, being closer at hand, were often the stronger in the comitia, and they sold the State to anyone who would stoop to buy the votes of the rabble that filled them.

Since the founder had set up ten _curiæ_ in each tribe, the whole Roman people, which was then contained within the walls, consisted of thirty _curiæ_. Each had its temples, its gods, its officers, its priests and its festivals. These festivals were called _compitalia_, and they corresponded to the _paganalia_ held in later times by the rural tribes.

When Servius made his new division, the thirty _curiæ_ could not be shared equally among his four tribes, and he was unwilling to interfere with them. They therefore became a further division of the inhabitants of Rome, quite independent of the tribes. In the case of the rural tribes and their members, however, there was no question of _curiæ_. The tribes had by then become a purely civil institution, and a new system of levying troops had been introduced, so the military divisions of Romulus were unnecessary. Thus, although every citizen was enrolled in a tribe, there were very many who were not members of a _curia_.

Servius made yet a third division, quite distinct from the two just described, and in its effects it became the most important of all. He distributed the whole Roman people into six classes, distinguished neither by place nor by person but by wealth. The first classes included the rich, the last the poor, and those in between people of moderate means. These six classes were subdivided into one hundred and ninety-three other bodies, called centuries. They were divided so that the first class alone held more than half of them, while the last held only one. Thus the class with the fewest members had the most centuries, and the whole of the last class counted as a single subdivision, although it alone included more than half the inhabitants of Rome.
